dossiers.title: Naming Words & Action Words
dossiers.brief: Open the pen tray and mark the evidence: nouns, verbs and adjectives.

cases.title: The Sleepy Witness
cases.sentence: The old dog sleeps in the garden.
clues: A noun names a person, a place, an animal or a thing.
Look for one animal and one place hiding in this sentence.
The two nouns are the animal 'dog' and the place 'garden'.
cases.explanation: A noun names a person, a place, an animal or a thing. In this case file, 'dog' is the animal and 'garden' is the place, so both take the NOUN pen. The other words describe or connect - they stay unmarked.

cases.title: The Library Clue
cases.sentence: My sister reads a funny book.
clues: A verb is an action word - it tells us what someone does.
What does the sister do? Find that action word, then find the two things.
Mark 'sister' and 'book' with the NOUN pen, and 'reads' with the VERB pen.
cases.explanation: The verb 'reads' is the action - it tells us what the sister does. 'Sister' is a person and 'book' is a thing, so they are nouns. 'Funny' describes the book, but this case did not ask for adjectives - good detectives only mark what the case asks for.

cases.title: The Kitchen Case
cases.sentence: The hungry cat drinks cold milk.
clues: An adjective describes a noun - it tells us more about it.
Which words tell us more about the cat and more about the milk?
Mark 'hungry' and 'cold' with the ADJECTIVE pen, then finish the nouns and the verb.
cases.explanation: 'Hungry' and 'cold' are adjectives - they describe the nouns 'cat' and 'milk'. 'Cat' and 'milk' are nouns, and 'drinks' is the action verb. Every marking pen in the tray was needed for this case.

cases.title: The Saturday Game
cases.sentence: Tom and his best friend play football in the park.
clues: Read the whole sentence first. Names like 'Tom' are nouns too.
This case has four nouns, one verb and one adjective. 'His' is not a noun - it just points to Tom.
Mark 'Tom', 'friend', 'football' and 'park' as NOUN, 'play' as VERB, and 'best' as ADJECTIVE.
cases.explanation: Names of people are nouns, so 'Tom' counts. 'Friend', 'football' and 'park' are also nouns - four in total. 'Play' is the action verb, and 'best' is the adjective describing the friend. 'His' only points at Tom, so it stays unmarked.

dossiers.title: The Word Order Desk
dossiers.brief: The sentences fell apart on the desk. Rebuild them word by word.

cases.title: The Broken Lunch Line
clues: English sentences usually start with the person - the subject.
Who eats? Start with 'We', then the action, then the food.
The order is: We - eat - apples - after school.
cases.explanation: An English sentence usually goes subject - verb - object: who, then the action, then the thing. 'We eat apples' follows that line, and 'after school' tells the time at the end.

cases.title: The Night Reader
clues: Start with the subject and its verb, then place the time words.
Time words like 'every night' usually come at the end - but there is another correct home for them.
Two orders are accepted here: 'She reads books every night.' or 'Every night she reads books.'
cases.explanation: Time words like 'every night' can come after the verb phrase: 'She reads books every night.' Or they can open the sentence: 'Every night, she reads books.' The bureau accepts both - this case file has two correct answers.

cases.title: The Bus Route
cases.sentence: She goes to school by bus.
acceptedAnswers: She goes to school by bus.
clues: The subject 'She' comes first, then the verb 'goes'.
Place comes before travel way: 'to school' comes before 'by bus'.
The full line is: She - goes - to school - by bus.
cases.rule: Rule 07 - Adverbial phrases at the end
cases.explanation: Adverbial phrase comes after the main clause here. 'She goes' is the main clause, and the phrases 'to school' (place) then 'by bus' (way) follow it.

cases.title: The Tea Question
clues: Questions in English borrow a helper: 'Do' opens the question.
After 'Do' comes the person, then the action, then the thing.
The order is: Do - you - like - green tea?
cases.explanation: In yes/no questions, the helper 'Do' jumps to the front: Do - you - like - green tea? The verb 'like' stays after the subject 'you', and the question mark card closes the case.

dossiers.title: The Review Vault
dossiers.brief: Mixed evidence from every desk. Marks and order both count.

cases.title: The Hidden Key
cases.sentence: Two young detectives found a heavy key under the old bridge.
clues: Sweep the sentence left to right: naming words, action word, describing words.
Watch out: 'Two' is a number, not an adjective in this case file.
NOUN: detectives, key, bridge. VERB: found. ADJECTIVE: young, heavy, old.
cases.explanation: 'Detectives', 'key' and 'bridge' are nouns; 'found' is the verb; 'young', 'heavy' and 'old' are adjectives. 'Two' looks like it describes the detectives, but numbers are not adjectives in this bureau - that was the trap.

cases.title: The Slow Door
cases.sentence: The quiet boy slowly opened the small door.
clues: Three pens, three jobs: naming, action, describing.
Careful: 'slowly' ends in -ly but it tells HOW the action happens - it is not one of the three pens here.
NOUN: boy, door. VERB: opened. ADJECTIVE: quiet, small. Leave 'slowly' unmarked.
cases.explanation: 'Boy' and 'door' are nouns, 'opened' is the verb, and 'quiet' and 'small' are adjectives. 'Slowly' describes the action, not a noun - words like that belong to another case file, so the pen tray correctly leaves it unmarked.

cases.title: The Long Afternoon
cases.sentence: The children play in the park after school.
acceptedAnswers: The children play in the park after school.
clues: Subject and verb make the engine of the sentence - build that first.
When a place and a time both wait at the end, the place steps in first.
The line reads: The children - play - in the park - after school.
cases.explanation: When both a place and a time come at the end, English puts the place first: 'in the park' before 'after school'. So the mended line is 'The children play in the park after school.'

cases.title: The Backyard Tree
cases.sentence: There is a big tree behind our house.
acceptedAnswers: There is a big tree behind our house.
clues: 'There is' is how English points at something that exists - keep the pair together at the front.
After 'There is' comes the thing you point at, with its describing word in front of it.
The line is: There - is - a big tree - behind our house.
cases.explanation: 'There is' points at something that exists: There is - a big tree - behind our house. The place phrase 'behind our house' closes the sentence, exactly like 'in the park' did in the last case.
